item.title: Swamped curl maintainers take low-level flaws public to survive vulnerability 'avalanche'
item.description: An "avalanche of vulnerability reports" is forcing curl to move lower-severity cases into public view, reserving private handling for high and critical flaws. From October 26, low and medium-severity reports should be filed in the open source data transfer tool's public GitHub repository, maintainer Daniel Stenberg said . "Security researchers in doubt can still submit the issue on HackerOne and we can tell them what severity we deem it to be. Over the last few years, over 90 percent of all submissions could quickly be assessed to be less than HIGH." Stenberg already shuttered curl's bug bounty scheme this year as AI-generated submissions piled work onto its security team. Stenberg has previously acknowledged that not all AI-assisted reports are bad, but the workload now demands another response. "This policy change is entirely triggered by the current avalanche of vulnerability reports that keep pouring in . We see no end to them and we do not anticipate this flood to decrease within the next several months. "We are struggling as a project as all key maintainers feel strained, overloaded and brought to the brink of what we can muster. We must act to survive. This is our next step in a survival strategy. It might not be our last. We aim to not drown." Public handling would let more people assess reports, develop fixes, write advisories, and check for related problems before releases ship, Stenberg said. Handling vulnerability reports publicly won't reduce the work per report, he admits, though it could spread the load and make the resulting lessons and documentation easier to find. At least that's the theory. Public disclosure also gives attackers more time to exploit flaws before fixes arrive. The maintainer agrees this is unfortunate yet unavoidable. "We limit this practice to less than HIGH for this reason: at least these problems are not terrible." Stenberg said researchers using AI are generating unusual option combinations unlikely to occur in real applications, then treating minor discrepancies as vulnerabilities. "We can't continue down this spiraling path with our sanity intact. We don't have the bandwidth, manpower or even will to handle a never-ending vulnerability reporting stream at this pace. I believe few software projects can stand this kind of prolonged high volume deluge for extended periods. Something needs to give way." ®

item.title: OneDrive loses bunch of Copilot shortcuts in File Explorer clear-out
item.description: Microsoft is pruning OneDrive's Copilot options from File Explorer's right-click menu, though the AI assistant isn't being shown the door entirely. The Windows giant will remove shortcuts for summarizing documents, generating FAQs, comparing files and images, explaining images, extracting text, and asking questions. The rollout begins in mid-November and is expected to finish by early December. "Ask Copilot" will remain. Microsoft's September 2025 announcement of the feature said: "We are bringing the power of AI directly into your daily file management experience. With just a few clicks, Copilot can help you summarize lengthy documents, generate an FAQ, compare files, or answer questions about your file." Users can still right-click a OneDrive file and select "Ask Copilot" to start a conversation with the file attached, or use the Copilot icon in File Explorer Home. The individual actions will also remain available in the OneDrive activity center. Adding a clutch of Copilot options with identical icons did little to make an already crowded menu easier to navigate. In its message on the subject, Microsoft said: "We're simplifying how people use Copilot with their OneDrive files in File Explorer." An extra click, yes, but at least you won't need a taller screen to view even more context menu options. Microsoft has stated that it intends to adopt a more thoughtful approach to how and where its AI assistant turns up in its product line. In March 2026, Windows boss Pavan Davuluri said : "We are reducing unnecessary Copilot entry points." File Explorer's crowded right-click menu seems as good a place to start as any. The File Explorer context menu is also undergoing an overhaul as part of Microsoft's attempt to make it less "cluttered and sluggish," to the point where users could opt to have it work a bit like it used to in Windows 10. ®

item.title: openEuler brings China's enterprise Linux ambitions to the desktop
item.description: Surprisingly few organizations were promoting Linux distros at Open Source Summit Europe. The only dedicated stands we found belonged to two Chinese projects, with openEuler occupying the larger booth. For users accustomed to Western enterprise distros, openEuler may be a less familiar name, but it has an impressive history. It's the modern free community version of Huawei's EulerOS, a version of which achieved official official UNIX™ certification . openEuler is no longer a solely Huawei project, though. Since then, it's been opened up, and it is now run by the OpenAtom Foundation . OpenAtom was co-founded in 2020 by Huawei along with some other big Chinese names, such as Alibaba, Baidu, and Tencent. Another of the co-founders was Inspur, which formerly developed its own distro, K/UX – a version of which also achieved official UNIX™ certification . Inspur K/UX won Unix certification in February 2016, and EulerOS seven months later. K/UX's Unix certification expired in 2019. A few months later, in May 2019, the US placed wider sanctions on Huawei . It is possible that the fresh restrictions on American sales prompted Huawei's interest in closer co-operation with other companies in the Chinese Linux space. As far as we can see, there were no further versions of K/UX after version 3. As additional motivation for cooperation, both EulerOS and K/UX were originally based on CentOS Linux, and of course, in December 2020, the CentOS Project announced it would shift its focus from CentOS Linux to CentOS Stream . The openEuler community has taken the platform in new directions. It has built its own stack of tools for developing, deploying, and running LLMs, called Intelligence BooM . It has a tool for migrating CentOS Linux systems to openEuler, called x2openEuler . As you would expect, it supports Kubernetes, as well as Docker and Podman, but it also has its own container engine called iSula (named after a species of ant ). Aware that it's less known outside Asia, at the Open Source Summit, OpenAtom was handing out copies of a special "Focus Guide" from Admin Magazine, which is also available as a free download . Some parts of this are also available online without registration, such as AI and the BooM Stack and Automating Migration to openEuler . openEuler has a dual-strand release cycle , akin to Ubuntu rather than the RHELatives, with LTS versions and more frequent "innovation releases." The current LTS is version 24.03, released in June 2024 , while the latest version is 26.09. There is a plethora of versions and editions available on the downloads page : the latest release is for x86-64 and 64-bit Arm. The LTS version adds support for RISC-V and LoongArch, and there are minimal versions for 32-bit Arm as well. The older 22.03 LTS was also available for SW-64, meaning the SunWay RISC processors that Register sister site The Next Platform looked at in 2016. The openEuler community has taken the platform in new directions. It has built its own stack of tools for developing, deploying, and running LLMs, called Intelligence BooM . It has a tool for migrating CentOS Linux systems to openEuler, called x2openEuler . As you would expect, it supports Kubernetes, as well as Docker and Podman, but it also has its own container engine called iSula (named after a species of ant ). Aware that it's less known outside Asia, at the Open Source Summit, OpenAtom was handing out copies of a special "Focus Guide" from Admin Magazine, which is also available as a free download . Some parts of this are also available online without registration, such as AI and the BooM Stack and Automating Migration to openEuler . openEuler has a dual-strand release cycle , akin to Ubuntu rather than the RHELatives, with LTS versions and more frequent "innovation releases." The current LTS is version 24.03, released in June 2024 , while the latest version is 26.09. There is a plethora of versions and editions available on the downloads page : the latest release is for x86-64 and 64-bit Arm. The LTS version adds support for RISC-V and LoongArch, and there are minimal versions for 32-bit Arm as well. The older 22.03 LTS was also available for SW-64, meaning the SunWay RISC processors that Register sister site The Next Platform looked at in 2016. As LWN put it last year , this is a "non-upstream kernel port." There are five types of installation ISO available: Offline Standard, Offline Everything (a hefty 24.9 GB), Network Install (a still significant 1.5 GB), and two variants of the desktop "DevStation" version – a basic one at 3.3 GB and an "everything" edition at 25 GB. We gave the DevStation a very quick whirl in VirtualBox. It boots into its own installation program called Heolleo , which offers the choice of Simplified Chinese or English. Installation took a while, as it automatically fetches updates as it goes. We ended up with a GNOME desktop configured for Chinese, but we opened Settings, typed "language" into the Search box, and picked English. After a reboot, we could read most of the desktop. Program groups and some other elements are still in Chinese, but it's navigable with a bit of guesswork. It's GNOME 49, with the Dash to Panel and Arc Menu extensions preinstalled for a slightly more familiar layout. Opening a terminal, we were greeted with: Welcome to 6.18.48-0.0.0.15.oe2609.x86_64 It also offers the Deepin Desktop Environment, UKUI (as seen in Ubuntu Kylin), MATE, Xfce, and the Kiran Desktop Environment , which is a new one to us. In places, the English-language materials for openEuler mention Chinese CPU makers rather than western ones – which is understandable, in context. Examples include processors from Hygon, a Chinese licensee of AMD designs , as well as Phytium and Kunpeng , which explain the Arm support on offer. In the western world, the Red Hat user community responded to the end of CentOS Linux by building new free distros that stay as close as they can to their progenitor: the Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux projects , rebuilt from Red Hat source code. Then, when the IBM subsidiary restricted access to that source to its customers in 2023, the Rocky and AlmaLinux projects started to diverge. Rocky aims for the closest possible RHEL compatibility, and its most visible innovation is that it's built its own new build service . It also found a clever workaround to get Red Hat's kernel source code. AlmaLinux still targets RHEL compatibility, but differentiates itself by retaining older device support and older CPU architectures after Red Hat drops them. Chinese vendors have responded very differently. Those offering CentOS Linux-based OSes clubbed together, dropped their rival versions and their UNIX compatibility efforts, and instead are working on new tools and subsystems. Much like European interest in digital sovereignty , this is in part due to the Trump administration. Half a decade after it was cut off from its upstream sources, the openEuler platform is thriving and growing, even if few in the western world pay any attention at all. ®

item.title: How going dual-native means VM/container co-existence and sovereign security in the AI era
item.description: Seasoned techies recall with nostalgia a simpler time when the “single-stack” model of enterprise computing held as the default approach to solving interoperability headaches. Back then IT decision-makers were prepared to forfeit some choice and flexibility in how they specified IT systems in return for the availability and manageability that came with a homogenous operating environment. With the subsequent rise of multi-clouds, application-specific hardware, ever-changing business requirements, and the race for AI, the old “one-size-fits-all” playbook has been largely abandoned. Most IT estates have embraced technological diversity, some by design, some through standardization, some by inertia. Modern enterprise environments have become innately heterogeneous – and innately complex. They run a diverse combo of system software, hardware devices, cloud services, legacy applications, et al . The advance of AI has brought standard CPUs, specialized GPUs, fast networking fabrics, distributed data pipelines, and new deployment models that span private clouds, public clouds, edge – and ever-pressing ROI expectations. But that doesn’t mean that companies’ existing applications and data simply disappear. One trying but inevitable outcome of rapid AI deployment is the so-called “VM-container divide”. This is where critical business applications tipped to transition to containers continue to run on virtual machines, because cloud-native services are taking precedence, nabbing container and Kubernetes availability. So companies face the challenge of operationalizing AI, without being forced into complex migrations or creating new infrastructure silos. Dealing with this technological schism poses acute challenges for IT management. Many new AI deployments are going straight to containers, while existing data and applications – which the AI needs to access – continue to run on VMs. Running separate stacks for VMs and containers creates a number of issues, such as duplicate capacity plans, separate support contracts, and fragmented governance. And after years of trying to get beyond the pitfalls of siloed data, exasperated enterprises are now having to deal with siloed infrastructure. Separately managed VM and container environments often mean inefficient resource utilization. This in turn can lead to “stranded capacity” – installed computing resources that cannot be used to support live workloads. VM clusters are frequently underutilized while container pools (like Kubernetes) are overprovisioned, with no easy way to share resources without manual intervention. Furthermore, VM/container infrastructure fragmentation can create an operations bottleneck for agentic AI. Infrastructure fragmentation can complicate the deployment, integration, governance, and scaling of agents thus making it harder to operationalize and scale agentic AI securely and consistently. item.dc:creator: James Hayes
item.content:encoded: Seasoned techies recall with nostalgia a simpler time when the “single-stack” model of enterprise computing held as the default approach to solving interoperability headaches. Back then IT decision-makers were prepared to forfeit some choice and flexibility in how they specified IT systems in return for the availability and manageability that came with a homogenous operating environment. With the subsequent rise of multi-clouds, application-specific hardware, ever-changing business requirements, and the race for AI, the old “one-size-fits-all” playbook has been largely abandoned. Most IT estates have embraced technological diversity, some by design, some through standardization, some by inertia. Modern enterprise environments have become innately heterogeneous – and innately complex. They run a diverse combo of system software, hardware devices, cloud services, legacy applications, et al . The advance of AI has brought standard CPUs, specialized GPUs, fast networking fabrics, distributed data pipelines, and new deployment models that span private clouds, public clouds, edge – and ever-pressing ROI expectations. But that doesn’t mean that companies’ existing applications and data simply disappear. One trying but inevitable outcome of rapid AI deployment is the so-called “VM-container divide”. This is where critical business applications tipped to transition to containers continue to run on virtual machines, because cloud-native services are taking precedence, nabbing container and Kubernetes availability. So companies face the challenge of operationalizing AI, without being forced into complex migrations or creating new infrastructure silos. Dealing with this technological schism poses acute challenges for IT management. Many new AI deployments are going straight to containers, while existing data and applications – which the AI needs to access – continue to run on VMs. Running separate stacks for VMs and containers creates a number of issues, such as duplicate capacity plans, separate support contracts, and fragmented governance. And after years of trying to get beyond the pitfalls of siloed data, exasperated enterprises are now having to deal with siloed infrastructure. Separately managed VM and container environments often mean inefficient resource utilization. This in turn can lead to “stranded capacity” – installed computing resources that cannot be used to support live workloads. VM clusters are frequently underutilized while container pools (like Kubernetes) are overprovisioned, with no easy way to share resources without manual intervention. Furthermore, VM/container infrastructure fragmentation can create an operations bottleneck for agentic AI. Infrastructure fragmentation can complicate the deployment, integration, governance, and scaling of agents thus making it harder to operationalize and scale agentic AI securely and consistently. When AI agents cannot autonomously communicate across environments, their utility droops from autonomous problem-solvers to plain localised macros. Containers are gaining because of the widespread embrace of AI-enabled applications. Eighty-five percent of IT executives polled by Nutanix’s most recent Enterprise Cloud Index survey think that AI is accelerating their organization’s adoption of containers in a meaningful way; 29 percent think it is speeding-up adoption “to a great extent”. “AI is accelerating the shift to containers because machine learning models require strict dependency packing, while critical applications and data remain spread across both virtualised and containerised environments,” says Harsha Kotikela, Senior Director of Product & Solutions Marketing at Nutanix. Agents are multi-tier by nature he explains. “Inference is typically GPU-intensive and container-based, while agents are often CPU-intensive and container-based, and existing enterprise applications and data largely remain in VM environments. The challenge is to bring these tiers together so agents can work with enterprise applications and data, without forcing migration or creating additional infrastructure silos.” The application landscape, meanwhile, has become just as diverse. Many organisations simultaneously operate traditional enterprise applications running on VMs, containerised apps, distributed AI applications and intelligent agents, with workloads deployed across private cloud, public cloud, and edge. Each environment has its own management tools, operational processes, security rules and governance models. “Management capability has struggled to scale up commensurately,” says Kotikela, but adding more consoles or building separate operational teams for every technology stack does not necessarily solve this complexity: “In many cases, it increases it.” However, Kotikela challenges the notion that the predicament enterprises face in straddling the VM-container divide is intractable. Rather, the challenge is to move towards a unified operating model that allows them to operationalize agentic AI while retaining flexibility across their existing and new environments. “Rather than trying to work around heterogeneity, the objective now should be to make heterogeneous environments operate consistently with purposeful policies,” Kotikela says. “This is where Nutanix's dual-native architecture comes in, enabling enterprises to operationalize agentic AI across container-based inference and agent workloads alongside existing VM-based applications and data, through a consistent operating model.” The reality is that the VM-to-container migration trend is sluggish, Kotikela suggests. Few enterprises are starting from scratch with containers. Many have long-established business applications on legacy architectures, on top of which they are building container-based applications, but mostly not to replace what they already have running on VMs. Rather, they are prolonging their VM investment. It’s customer interest that’s informed how Nutanix provisions a governed, dual-native architecture through its Nutanix Cloud Platform – NCP – which runs traditional VMs and containerised/Kubernetes-based AI workloads concurrently on a single, consistent infrastructure. NCP’s hybrid-cloud infrastructure foundation unifies compute, storage, virtualisation and management across on-premises resources, public clouds and edge. It works in concert with Nutanix Enterprise AI (NAI), which provides the software capabilities to deploy, govern, and scale AI workloads. Technology partnerships are vital to building AI support functionality into Nutanix's AI portfolio, explains Kotikela. “Nutanix and NVIDIA work together to provide an integrated platform for enterprise AI, combining Nutanix’s hybrid-cloud infrastructure and software with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AI software. Nutanix Enterprise AI simplifies the deployment, management, and secure operation of AI models, integrating with NVIDIA NIM and NeMo microservices to support enterprise AI inference and agentic AI workflows.” Meanwhile, “Nutanix Kubernetes Platform provides the foundation for managing Kubernetes environments, while Nutanix Unified Storage delivers the high-performance data access required by AI workloads. Together, these capabilities help enterprises deploy and scale AI while maintaining control over their infrastructure, models, and data.” Stacks of opportunity “In an ideal IT world you do not want to have to manage two different operational stacks – but the world of IT is rarely ‘ideal’,” Kotikela points out. “So you have to approach the challenge from a realistic perspective. You cannot bend your current stacks to a different reality without the risk of something breaking, and there’s no sense in that.” He adds: “A platform that unifies VMs and containers improves developer time-to-value by getting rid of those infrastructure silos, and providing a single control plane.” Rather than development teams having to manage separate pipelines for existing VMs and

item.title: Enterprises blow nearly a third of software budgets on upgrades they never asked for
item.description: Enterprises say nearly a third of their software budgets goes on upgrades, migrations, and licensing changes they wouldn't have chosen, according to research suggesting that keeping vendors happy has become an expensive business. The study , conducted by Censuswide for software support provider Origina and published with Thinkers50, surveyed 2,018 senior IT decision-makers in the US and UK. Respondents put the average share at 28 percent. And customers aren't necessarily getting anything better for their money. Some 95 percent of respondents said they had paid for at least one vendor-driven change in the past three years despite expecting worse reliability, performance, or value. The most recent vendor-driven change cost respondents' organizations an average of $12.87 million. Origina calls this the "software tax," but unlike most taxes, it comes with the added pleasure of potentially making your IT systems worse. The costs don't stop at software either. According to the survey, 91 percent of respondents said their organizations had retired working hardware in the past three years to meet software support deadlines, sacrificing an estimated 1.65 years of remaining useful life on average. Then there's the small matter of finding people to carry out all these supposedly essential changes. Some 84 percent said experienced engineers were regularly diverted from other projects to handle vendor-driven upgrades and migrations. That leaves less time for the work businesses actually want done, including the AI projects that software vendors themselves have spent the past few years telling everyone they urgently need. Asked about the last time an AI or data project was delayed, paused, or canceled, 90 percent said vendor-driven costs contributed at least moderately. While customers might be tempted to tell their suppliers where to stick their next upgrade, many apparently don't feel they have much choice. Some 76 percent said they have little negotiating leverage with their major software vendors. Origina founder and CEO Tomás O'Leary reckons customers have been backed into a corner. "When the alternative to an unwanted upgrade is losing support on systems the business runs on, saying yes is often a rational response. That's exactly the problem," he said. "The market has left some of the most experienced technology leaders in the world with little room to refuse, and that cost shows up in budgets, in engineering time and in innovation that never gets funded." The findings also suggest that IT bosses are getting rather fed up with the arrangement. Some 91 percent backed legislation that would give enterprise software customers protections comparable to those enjoyed by long-term residential tenants, while 82 percent supported software maintenance requirements similar to EU hardware repairability rules. Some 84 percent said experienced engineers were regularly diverted from other projects to handle vendor-driven upgrades and migrations. Asked about the last time an AI or data project was delayed, paused, or canceled, 90 percent said vendor-driven costs contributed at least moderately. Some 76 percent said they have little negotiating leverage with their major software vendors. Origina founder and CEO Tomás O'Leary reckons customers have been backed into a corner. Origina has a commercial interest in the argument: it sells independent support for enterprise software, offering customers an alternative to vendors' own maintenance and upgrade arrangements. Still, the findings suggest plenty of customers feel they're spending millions following their suppliers' priorities rather than their own. ®

item.title: The dangers of letting tech billionaires shape our world
item.description: As SpaceX impacts Ukraine and AI-generated music divides artists and fans, critics are asking what happens when technology has too much control over our lives This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. Sign up to receive it here Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you while sitting in front of Roy Lichtenstein’s monumental Drowning Girl, on view in New York City . Today in tech, we’re discussing the perils of Elon Musk’s one-man global infrastructure, AI-generated music and a Guardian AI conference in Paris. Continue reading...

item.title: Labor and the Coalition are poised to take a reckless gamble on AI. Haven’t they realised community support has collapsed? | Edward Santow and Sarah Sacher
item.description: Australian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at hand Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Australia’s major political parties are edging towards rare consensus. Labor and the Coalition increasingly want to take a major bet on artificial intelligence. Yet, just as the parties are coming together, the Australian community is running the other way. Last year, only 30% of Australians believed the benefits of AI outweighed the risks. In 2026, community trust in AI appears to be falling even further. Continue reading...

item.title: HPE to launch AI straight to the Moon
item.description: Forget space datacenters. Before the end of the year, HPE will have AI running on the Moon. This isn’t some exec’s loony fantasy either. HPE has been building orbital compute platforms for the International Space Station (ISS) for years. Now, it’s sending its fourth-gen Spaceborne Computer to the Moon aboard Astrolab’s Flex Lunar Innovation Platform (FLIP) lunar rover. Part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program, the rover is set to be deployed near the Moon’s south pole by the Voyager Technologies Griffin-1 lander later this year. Assuming a safe landing on the surface, FLIP will serve as a test bed for a range of emerging technologies including HPE’s latest space-faring compute platform. Specifically, Spaceborne Computer 4, which for the sake of brevity we’ll just call SBC4, will carry out a number of AI and HPC-centric experiments during the rover’s year long mission on the lunar pole. What we know about SBC4 so far The actual silicon powering SBC4 is still a bit of a mystery. We’re told the reason for the secrecy largely comes down to the high-risk nature of the mission. If the hardware fails, HPE’s compute partner doesn’t want their name tied to it. No guts but for the glory, we suppose, though Kioxia doesn't seem too worried. What we do know is that it is equipped with a low-power central processing unit, a graphics processor, and will be equipped with a pair of mirrored Kioxia SSDs totaling 1 TB of capacity. That said, while it'll be among the most powerful computers on the Moon, it's still a pretty small system. The FLIP rover doesn't have an unlimited power or thermal budget. The rover's radiators can only dissipate so much heat. Measuring in at around 5x10 inches and about an inch thick, while not a particularly big system, it's still large enough to house any number of existing compute platforms. For all we know, it could be powered by Nvidia’s GB10, AMD’s Xilinx Versal AI, or the guts of an old smartphone. We won't know until the thing powers up. Less of a mystery is what SBC4 will be running and where. NASA plans to run a series of tuned LLM tests on the system, including a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system to assist with searching and interpreting onboard documents. Additionally, the system will be tasked with running machine learning algorithms against camera and LiDAR data. However, without knowing how large these LLMs are, it’s hard to infer the nature of the underlying hardware. We’re told to expect more details about the chips powering SBC4 once it’s up and running. Alongside AI, SBC4 will also run several high performance computing (HPC) benchmarks designed to push the system to its limits. These benchmarks include high performance Linpack (HPL) and high performance conjugate gradient (HPCG), which means HPE and Astrolab will soon hold the distinction of the first Top500 submission made from a celestial body. item.content:encoded: Forget space datacenters. Before the end of the year, HPE will have AI running on the Moon. This isn’t some exec’s loony fantasy either. HPE has been building orbital compute platforms for the International Space Station (ISS) for years. Now, it’s sending its fourth-gen Spaceborne Computer to the Moon aboard Astrolab’s Flex Lunar Innovation Platform (FLIP) lunar rover. Part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program, the rover is set to be deployed near the Moon’s south pole by the Voyager Technologies Griffin-1 lander later this year. Assuming a safe landing on the surface, FLIP will serve as a test bed for a range of emerging technologies including HPE’s latest space-faring compute platform. Specifically, Spaceborne Computer 4, which for the sake of brevity we’ll just call SBC4, will carry out a number of AI and HPC-centric experiments during the rover’s year long mission on the lunar pole. What we know about SBC4 so far The actual silicon powering SBC4 is still a bit of a mystery. We’re told the reason for the secrecy largely comes down to the high-risk nature of the mission. If the hardware fails, HPE’s compute partner doesn’t want their name tied to it. No guts but for the glory, we suppose, though Kioxia doesn't seem too worried. What we do know is that it is equipped with a low-power central processing unit, a graphics processor, and will be equipped with a pair of mirrored Kioxia SSDs totaling 1 TB of capacity. That said, while it'll be among the most powerful computers on the Moon, it's still a pretty small system. The FLIP rover doesn't have an unlimited power or thermal budget. The rover's radiators can only dissipate so much heat. Measuring in at around 5x10 inches and about an inch thick, while not a particularly big system, it's still large enough to house any number of existing compute platforms. For all we know, it could be powered by Nvidia’s GB10, AMD’s Xilinx Versal AI, or the guts of an old smartphone. We won't know until the thing powers up. Less of a mystery is what SBC4 will be running and where. NASA plans to run a series of tuned LLM tests on the system, including a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system to assist with searching and interpreting onboard documents. Additionally, the system will be tasked with running machine learning algorithms against camera and LiDAR data. However, without knowing how large these LLMs are, it’s hard to infer the nature of the underlying hardware. We’re told to expect more details about the chips powering SBC4 once it’s up and running. Alongside AI, SBC4 will also run several high performance computing (HPC) benchmarks designed to push the system to its limits. These benchmarks include high performance Linpack (HPL) and high performance conjugate gradient (HPCG), which means HPE and Astrolab will soon hold the distinction of the first Top500 submission made from a celestial body. Not only do HPE’s systems power some of the fastest supercomputers on Earth, but they could soon hold the number one spot on the Moon — not that that’s a particularly high bar. Beyond bragging rights, a workload like HPL could have other benefits like helping to keep the rover from icing over during the roughly 14-day-long night cycles the rover will repeatedly endure over the course of its mission. Hardening SBC4 for the Moon The Rover and by extension SBC4 will have to contend with extreme vibration stresses during launch and landing, wild temperature swings, not to mention cosmic rays and solar radiation since the Moon lacks the thick atmosphere and magnetic field that shields terrestrial compute. But, as it turns out, radiation might not be as big a problem as you’d think. According to Fernandez, SBC4 is largely assembled from off-the-shelf components, including the solid state drives. The compute platform is using standard Kioxia BG6 M.2 drives with the main line of protection being a software RAID 1. “It’s a silent mirror. The boot order is to try this and if something has happened to it, go here,” Mark Fernandez, HPE’s chief scientist of space tech and solutions, explained. “With our nine years' experience in the Space Station using drives, we’ve even convinced them we don’t need to do anything special for space.” However, this wasn’t always the thinking. As we reported at the time, early Spaceborne Computers suffered from high SSD failure rates. But as it turned out, so did the same drives deployed terrestrially. The cause of the failures wasn’t cosmic rays or energetic particles from the Sun, but rather bad capacitors, he explained. “I’ve had zero SSD failure since 2019.” While off-the-shelf electronics are surprisingly radiation resistant — at least within FLIP’s mission parameters — HPE has invested heavily in software based redundancy and recovery. Fernandez calls this “hardware hardening in software.” The idea being that the spare CPU cycles are used to continuously monitor and compare hardware metrics against a state table. If a parameter exceeds the specified threshold, SBC4 will take action to protect itself. “At a high level, I say, I like to be running at full speed. I can't do that. I'll run at a slower speed. If I can't do that, I'd like to be booted, but not running anything, and then maybe the server will recover. And worst case, I'd like to be powered down rather than get destroyed,” he explained. At the edge of the edge FLIP is primarily intended as a proof of concept vehicle, which is to say it’s a test bed for technologies that may eventually find their way to the Moon on other missions. The inclusion of SBC4 reflects the realities of operating at the far edge of Earth’s orbit. The latency between Earth and the Moon is nowhere near as bad as Mars's up to 44 minute round-trip communication time, but even 2.5 seconds makes real-time control from Houston, or in this case Astrolab’s mission control, which by the way is also powered by HPE's Greenlake Private Cloud stack, in Hawthorne, California a bit unwieldy. Further complicating matters is the bandwidth afforded the rover. When Artemis 2 traveled around the Moon earlier this year, astronauts weren’t able to send back high-res photographs in real time due to the lack of bandwidth. It was only after the mission was on its way back to Earth that they were able to establish a big enough pipe to transmit the full-res images. For this reason, SBC4 is designed to operate “at the edge of the edge,” Fernandez said. Given the bandwidth constraints, it’s far easier to process as much of the data and telemetry gathered by the rover’s array of cameras, lidars, and environmental sensors locally. “It’s important to ship back insight to Earth rather than all the raw data whenever possible. So having the edge compute capability to process the raw data locally, save on bandwidth back to Earth,” Astrolab CEO Jaret Matthews said. Matthews isn’t the only one to share this perspective. Earlier this year, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang described the challenges and opportunities of space-based computing with analysts during the company’s Q1 earnings call. "There are many different computing problems that really want to be done in space," he said at the time. "One of the best use cases of GPUs in space is imaging. To be able to do imaging at very large, very high resolutions, extremely large scales and very, very fast, it's hard to do that by sending petabytes and petabytes of imaging data back here on Earth and doing that work, it's easier just to do it out in space." Though others' ambitions are far greater. Google, Amazon, and SpaceX are all touting orbital datacenters powered by the Sun as the answer to terrestrial power constraints — Elon Musk wants you to believe he'll eventually be manufacturing deep-space datacenters on the Moon and lobbing them into the far reaches of the solar system using mass drivers — the economics of getting those bit barns into low Earth orbit remain unproven and so far unviable. item.title: 'Password1' and a forgotten test account land Welsh outfits in hot water
item.description: A test account protected by "Password1" helped an intruder steal personal data relating to 3,300 people, mostly children, in a ransomware attack that has drawn regulatory rebukes for two Welsh organizations. The Information Commission's Office (ICO) issued reprimands rather than fines to Ogi Networks Limited (ONL) and the Local Government Data Unit – Wales, also known as Data Cymru. According to the ICO, altnet ONL provided server and connectivity infrastructure, licensing, and support to Data Cymru, which helps public bodies across Wales make effective use of data. On November 1, 2024, Data Cymru suffered a ransomware attack after a miscreant exploited a test account called Test2 to infiltrate its network and encrypt 182.7 GB of data housed in a file server and an internal database server. "Before deploying the ransomware, the threat actor exfiltrated 42 GB of data from a primary domain controller, a file server and an SQL server," the ICO said on Tuesday in its reprimand of ONL [PDF]. ONL told the ICO it created the test account on January 13, 2012, during its initial project for Data Cymru. "ONL confirmed that the creation of the 'Test2' account was likely intended to test user account access before migrating 'real' users to its services," the ICO said. "When it was created, the 'Test2' account was given the password of 'Password1'." The ICO cited Bitwarden's password strength tool, which rated "Password1" as "very weak" and estimated a cracking time of less than a second. "The local administrator accounts on the three impacted systems all had the same password. This meant that once one system had been breached, the local account hashes could be collected and used by the threat actor to authenticate access to other systems on the Data Cymru network," the regulator added. "ONL confirmed that it did not carry out any reviews of local administrator accounts following their initial deployment. This meant these accounts remained active, regardless of whether they were used, and continued to use the same default passwords set at the time of their creation in January 2012, as part of ONL's initial project with Data Cymru, for more than 12.5 years." The data watchdog reprimanded ONL under Article 32 of the UK GDPR because it failed to put in place "appropriate technical and organisational measures" to ensure processing systems and services were safe, and it didn't regularly assess or evaluate those measures. It found ONL had no auditing procedures to review user accounts within Data Cymru's Active Directory. The ICO's separate reprimand of Data Cymru [PDF] also detailed failures in its security arrangements. "Password1 is not an appropriate password, it is a wide-open door to nefarious actors," said ICO head of investigations David Doodson. "This incident shows how a single weak password, attached to an account that was no longer needed, can leave the door open to a serious cyber-attack that can affect thousands. "This incident shows how a single weak password, attached to an account that was no longer needed, can leave the door open to a serious cyber-attack that can affect thousands. "The responsibility for these failures did not sit with one organisation alone. ONL created the test account whilst Data Cymru retained overall control of its network, including the ability to instruct ONL to create or remove accounts. Neither had put in place sufficiently clear and effective measures to ensure that old accounts were routinely identified and removed." ®

item.title: Google Cloud says a 'power event' caused today's outage
item.description: UPDATED Google Cloud has blamed a “power event” for taking down multiple online products for customers in Western Europe, and is pledging to restore normal service within the hour. The unplanned downtime for customers began at 0608 UTC when europe-west-2-b, one of three local availability zones in the London region, started playing up. According to an update on its status page , Google Cloud said at 1158 UTC that full recovery workloads should be “completed, tentatively” by 1300 UTC. Customers can expect another update at that point, with Google either giving the thumbs up, thumbs sideways or having to admit engineers are still working on a fix. Services that went AWOL included BigQuery Data TransferService, Cloud Filestore, Cloud Run, Google App Engine, Google Cloud NetApp Volumes, Google Kubernetes Engine, and Managed Service for Apache Kafka. So what caused online services to melt at customers including Lloyds Bank, HSBC, Royal Mail, Rightmove, DPD, BT, Screwfix and Revolut? Power. "A power event caused an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated. We are seeing the recovery of services and are prioritizing the recovery of existing workloads.Customers may not be able to yet create new workloads." The Register has asked Google for further elucidation but it said the only information is available on the status page. The "fragility" of the cloud model is again on display, Dr Amro Al-Said Ahmad , a lecturer in computer science at Keele University told The Register . He estimates that a total of 38 services were down and out for the count. "The incident highlights the dependency effect of modern cloud ecosystems. When a core cloud region experiences failures, the impact extends far beyond the directly affected services. Applications, APIs, databases, authentication systems, payment platforms, analytics pipelines, and third-party SaaS products that depend on those services can all experience cascading failures." "A problem in a single cloud region can therefore propagate through an entire digital supply chain, affecting organisations that are several layers removed from the original outage. While this is a regional outage centered on europe-west2, the breadth of affected services highlights a key cloud engineering lesson: resilience is not achieved by simply moving to the cloud. True resilience requires designing for regional failures through multi-region deployments, workload portability, and tested disaster recovery procedures." Updated at 17.37 UTC on October 20, 2026, to add: Google's status page says it mostly ironed out the wrinkles at 14.03 UTC and normal service resumed for the majority of customers. "The issue with impacted GCP products has been mitigated for most of the customers and it is believed to be affecting currently a very small number of customers and our Engineering Team is working on it." "No further updates will be provided here. We will publish an analysis of this incident once we have completed our inter

item.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
item.description: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal . That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI. Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software company Continue reading...

item.title: Bullhorn sees red after cyberattack knocks recruitment platform offline
item.description: Bullhorn is the latest tech giant finding itself on the wrong end of a cyberattack, forcing the recruitment software provider to shut down its platform while it investigates. The US-based company, which serves more than 10,000 customers worldwide, says its systems are now back online in the UK, US, and Australia. Unfortunately for customers hoping to get back to work, online doesn't necessarily mean working. In its latest status update, published on Tuesday , Bullhorn confirmed that some users were still struggling with single sign-on (SSO), password resets, and customizations, while several products continued to report degraded performance. Things started going sideways on Friday, October 16, when Bullhorn flagged problems getting job postings onto Indeed. By the following morning, the platform was suffering a full-blown outage, and Bullhorn confirmed later that day that it was dealing with something rather more serious than a technical hiccup. "We have detected a cyber incident on the Bullhorn Platform. We have temporarily disabled access to our systems in order to contain the activity while we investigate further," the company said, noting that it had roped in cybersecurity specialists from CrowdStrike to help investigate the attack and restore its services. For recruitment agencies using Bullhorn, the outage meant losing access to candidate records, job applications, placements and, in some cases, the systems used to get people paid. Services began returning on Monday, but recovery has been anything but seamless. As of Tuesday morning, Bullhorn's status page still listed degraded performance across several products, including its automation tools, Talent Platform, Onboarding365 and Time & Expense. While Bullhorn is making progress getting customers back into their accounts, it has yet to answer arguably the bigger question: whether the attackers stole anything. In its customer FAQ , it said a forensic investigation is ongoing, and has not yet determined whether attackers exfiltrated customer data. Bullhorn says it will contact affected customers if the investigation finds their information was compromised, and it also warned people to watch out for opportunistic crooks looking to exploit the chaos. "Threat actors may pose as Bullhorn personnel via email, text, or phone calls, using the incident as a pretext to request credentials or sensitive information," it warned on Tuesday, stressing that its employees would never ask customers to disclose passwords, multi-factor authentication codes, or verification tokens. The company has also required password resets for users who don’t log in through SSO, while customers using API integrations have been instructed to rotate their credentials. The cause of the intrusion remains unknown, and Bullhorn has not publicly identified the attackers or confirmed whether ransomware was involved. The company didn’t respond to The Register ’s questions at publication time. The outage may be coming to an end, but B

item.title: Microsoft admits that Always On VPN problems were not fixed in the October Security Update
item.description: Microsoft has been forced to admit that the Always On VPN glitch – which it said it had fixed in an update on October 13 – was not actually fixed after all. We've all been there. You fix that bug, or tweak the configuration setting, and you're pleased with yourself, but it turns out it didn't take, and you have to send the "er, about that fix" follow-up email of shame. The same has happened to Microsoft. After proudly declaring the problem resolved as part of its last security update , the company had to roll back its triumphant trumpeting to a sad little parp from a clown's horn in the message WI1482218: "This disclosure was mistakenly updated to Resolved status on October 13, 2026. We have returned its status to Mitigated. "We apologize for any inconvenience or confusion." The bug in question concerns the operating system's Always On VPN functionality, a useful bit of code that quietly opens a VPN connection in the background without tiresome prompts for authentication. It dates back to Windows 10, and Microsoft alerted administrators to problems after the September 2026 Windows security update inadvertently broke it. The issue affects Windows 11 versions from 24H2 through 26H2. The problem could occur when the VPN was set to try a different connection method if the initial connection failed (Microsoft gave the example of using automatic protocol selection with IKEv2 and SSTP). According to Microsoft: "Affected VPN connections might remain in a 'Connecting' state or repeatedly attempt to connect without succeeding. Subsequent connection attempts might also display the error: 'The specified port is already in use'." This is not ideal for administrators. The workaround Microsoft highlighted back on October 13 was to change from automatic protocol selection to a single protocol, which would at least get affected users up and running. The workaround remains the same. The bad news is that, because last week's fix did not work, affected administrators will need to apply the workaround for a bit longer. Microsoft claimed, "A resolution for this issue is planned to be included in an update to be released in the coming weeks." ®

item.title: Whitehall shuts the front door on digital ID but leaves the back open
item.description: Britain's national digital ID scheme may be dead, but Whitehall appears to have forgotten to tell the infrastructure. Despite the government scrapping its controversial plans , officials told MPs on Monday that work continues on GOV.UK One Login, digital wallets, and a growing collection of digital credentials designed to help people prove who they are. The abandoned scheme was one of Keir Starmer's flagship policies, originally pitched as a compulsory digital ID card to crack down on illegal working. Privacy campaigners weren't impressed, warning of surveillance and government overreach, and ministers eventually made it voluntary before Andy Burnham, decided to bin the whole thing. But scrapping the scheme hasn't dented Whitehall's digital identity ambitions. Officials told MPs this week that more than 80 types of documents are earmarked for the government's digital wallet, including proof of benefits, driving test certificates, and Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) certificates. That's quite a lot of paperwork for something that's supposedly dead. The revelations came during a Public Accounts Committee hearing on Monday, where MPs wanted to know what exactly had been scrapped. "But is it not the case, based on the answers you've given us this afternoon, that the infrastructure of digital ID in the public sector is still being pursued?" asked Sarah Green, Liberal Democrat MP for Chesham and Amersham. Susannah Storey, DCMS permanent secretary, was keen to draw a line between the national scheme ministers had scrapped and the digital identity projects Whitehall had no intention of abandoning. One Login already allows people to prove who they are online, she said, but "that is not the same as a national digital identity strategy." Rod Latham, DCMS director for cybersecurity and digital identity, had a convenient explanation for why so much of digital ID was still standing: the government had only scrapped plans for a new identity product. "We already had One Login and the Gov Wallet," he told MPs, adding that work on the digital identity trust framework was also underway before the national scheme was announced. Whitehall isn't wasting time putting that technology to use, with officials confirming that testing is already underway to enable digital credentials to work with private businesses. Natalie Jones, the senior responsible owner for GOV.UK One Login, revealed that the government had opened a testing environment for private sector providers to integrate with its digital wallet technology. This would let people use digital driving licenses to prove their age in pubs , collect parcels, or verify their identity online. "We've got a bit of a chicken and egg situation. A digital driving license is only useful if there are people ready and shops and businesses ready to receive it,” Jones said, noting that further testing is planned for December, with a national rollout of digital driving licenses targeted for 2027. item.dc:creator: Carly Page
item.content:encoded: Britain's national digital ID scheme may be dead, but Whitehall appears to have forgotten to tell the infrastructure. Despite the government scrapping its controversial plans , officials told MPs on Monday that work continues on GOV.UK One Login, digital wallets, and a growing collection of digital credentials designed to help people prove who they are. The abandoned scheme was one of Keir Starmer's flagship policies, originally pitched as a compulsory digital ID card to crack down on illegal working. Privacy campaigners weren't impressed, warning of surveillance and government overreach, and ministers eventually made it voluntary before Andy Burnham, decided to bin the whole thing. But scrapping the scheme hasn't dented Whitehall's digital identity ambitions. Officials told MPs this week that more than 80 types of documents are earmarked for the government's digital wallet, including proof of benefits, driving test certificates, and Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) certificates. That's quite a lot of paperwork for something that's supposedly dead. The revelations came during a Public Accounts Committee hearing on Monday, where MPs wanted to know what exactly had been scrapped. "But is it not the case, based on the answers you've given us this afternoon, that the infrastructure of digital ID in the public sector is still being pursued?" asked Sarah Green, Liberal Democrat MP for Chesham and Amersham. Susannah Storey, DCMS permanent secretary, was keen to draw a line between the national scheme ministers had scrapped and the digital identity projects Whitehall had no intention of abandoning. One Login already allows people to prove who they are online, she said, but "that is not the same as a national digital identity strategy." Rod Latham, DCMS director for cybersecurity and digital identity, had a convenient explanation for why so much of digital ID was still standing: the government had only scrapped plans for a new identity product. "We already had One Login and the Gov Wallet," he told MPs, adding that work on the digital identity trust framework was also underway before the national scheme was announced. Whitehall isn't wasting time putting that technology to use, with officials confirming that testing is already underway to enable digital credentials to work with private businesses. Natalie Jones, the senior responsible owner for GOV.UK One Login, revealed that the government had opened a testing environment for private sector providers to integrate with its digital wallet technology. This would let people use digital driving licenses to prove their age in pubs , collect parcels, or verify their identity online. "We've got a bit of a chicken and egg situation. A digital driving license is only useful if there are people ready and shops and businesses ready to receive it,” Jones said, noting that further testing is planned for December, with a national rollout of digital driving licenses targeted for 2027. MPs also pressed officials on privacy, particularly whether citizens would have to consent before their information was shared between government departments. "In the confines of digital ID used in digital services, then consent is the model," said Christine Bellamy, interim director general for digital products at the Government Digital Service. There's a catch, of course. Government departments can already share data without asking permission, and officials couldn't quite explain how that squares with their promises about consent. "The strategy needs to be fully finished," Bellamy admitted, which might not be the reassurance MPs were hoping for. Jones insisted that One Login was "not a big data lake," saying it stores identity information separately and cannot see what users do inside government services. "One Login does not issue a single identifier to people," she added. Rupert Lowe MP remained unconvinced, warning that Britain could end up getting digital ID "by the back door rather than the front door." Officials maintained that the canceled national scheme was fundamentally different from the services still being developed, and that people would retain alternatives to digital identification. National digital ID may be officially dead, but between One Login, digital wallets, and dozens of planned credentials, Whitehall still has plenty of identity-related work to keep it busy. ®

item.title: UK finance watchdog wants firms to report AI failures and close calls
item.description: The UK's financial regulator says firms' incident reporting must cover significant AI failures and near-misses as increasingly autonomous systems raise new risks. Speaking at Bloomberg's UK Policy Series on Monday, Financial Conduct Authority chief data, information and intelligence officer Jessica Rusu said the regulator wants Britain to lead safe AI adoption in financial services. Greater autonomy, however, requires clear accountability. "Poorly governed AI can create consumer harm, cyber vulnerabilities, and operational failures, potentially at much greater speed and scale," she said. "Our rules already require firms to report major incidents, and that must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses. As the AI Minister has recognized, near-miss reporting for agentic AI is becoming a national security priority. It is a regulatory priority too." The UK punches above its weight in financial services. The sector contributed £223.6 billion to the UK economy in 2025 , or 8 percent of national output. That share was the fourth highest among OECD countries. Last week, UK artificial intelligence minister Kanishka Narayan said the government plans to work with Parliament and technical experts to assess how it could strengthen the regime to better protect Britain from AI-driven cyber threats and loss-of-control risks. "That includes identifying and reporting on serious incidents and near misses, including reducing AI-driven risk across essential services, and ensuring serious AI incidents can be properly reviewed," he said. Steven Adler, co-founder and chief scientist of independent nonprofit Guidelight AI Standards, also told MPs last week that AI oversight could learn from aviation, where reporting of near-misses is mandatory in most jurisdictions. "The way this works in aviation is that you not only want to learn about the serious crashes where someone has in fact died; you want to learn about the near-misses, because you can learn from those and help avoid them in the future," he said. However, the government has yet to commit to adding AI-specific measures to the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill. Alexandra Jones, Director General for Growth, Science and International at the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, told MPs last week that amendments remain under consideration. In January, the House of Commons Treasury Committee called on financial regulators to conduct stress tests to ensure businesses are ready for AI-driven market shocks. The committee said there should be clear lines of accountability when AI systems produce harmful or unfair outcomes. ®

item.title: Google cloud failure hits millions as UK courts and banks knocked offline
item.description: Services restored for most users, but power fault stalled hearings and left Revolut, Lloyds and HSBC customers unable to pay or move money An outage at Google’s cloud services in the UK has caused widespread disruption, hitting courts and leaving millions of customers unable to access or send cash at banks including Lloyds, HSBC and Revolut. Google blamed a “power event” for the failure at its London-based Cloud computing operations on Tuesday, which affected its “europe-west2-b zone”. Continue reading...

item.title: Google Cloud's London zones takes a nap, multiple services disrupted
item.description: UPDATED Google Cloud customers in Western Europe are waking up to severe disruption affecting multiple services and, as yet, there is no estimated time of recovery. The europe-west-2-b is one of three local availability zones in the London region, intended to help protect against hardware or regional failures. The downtime began at 0608 UTC, meaning customers need more than a coffee to feel OK about today. According to Google Cloud’s status page : “Multiple Google Cloud services are experiencing elevated errors and intermittent network failures in europe-west2 region.” BigQuery Data TransferService, Cloud Filestore, Cloud Run, Google App Engine, Google Cloud NetApp Volumes, Google Kubernetes Engine, and Managed Service for Apache Kafka are all impacted, the tech biz confirmed. “Our engineering team continues to investigate the issue,” Google added. “We apologize to all who are affected by the disruption.” Techies on Reddit said the interruption was having a cascading affect on multiple suppliers. One said: “ oh man the classic one zone takes a nap and your non-HA service is in it.” “Loads of stuff seems to be down, DNS somewhere,” mused another. Over on the platform formerly known as Twitter, customers weren’t any happier - but that’s par for the course for people that use Elon Musk’s X. “Major GCP incident affecting Europe regions, good start to the day,” said one . According to Down Detector , multiple customers are caught up including Lloyds Bank, HSBC, Royal Mail, Rightmove, DPD, BT, Screwfix and Revolut. “We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe. We’ve been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused,” said Revolut . Workarounds? “None for now now,” Google said. It plans to update customers at around 0930 UTC. ® Updated at 10.18 UTC on October 20, 2026, to add: Google has updated its status page to say Studio is not impacted by this outage and told customers looking for a workaround: "If feasible, the impacted customer may try to migrate their workload impacted to another available location."

item.title: London’s mobile networks fall to bottom of Europe’s capital league
item.description: London's mobile network performance has slipped behind other European capitals as operators struggle to add capacity fast enough to meet demand. The city ranked seventh out of 18 in the continent for median download speed in 2021, but traffic has since expanded faster than available capacity. Other metropolises have improved; London now has the slowest speeds and the highest latency under load, according to mobile network testing firm Ookla . The research points to obstacles mobile operators face in adding extra capacity: applications for new street masts in London have fallen since 2022, and about three quarters of those filed since 2019 were refused. The Big Smoke was among the first European capitals to get 5G coverage, yet when Ookla's Q3 2026 tests found the city now has the slowest median download speed (109.43 Mbps), the slowest median upload speed (11.40 Mbps) and the highest latency under load - a measure of how the network copes with heavy use. Ookla's records show London’s 5G medina speed peaked at 200 Mbps in Q2 2021, fell as low as 102 Mbps in Q3 2023, then recovered slightly. Paris, by contrast, has stayed above 225 Mbps since mid-2021. The cause is congestion. In Central London, performance slumps on weekdays as commuters arrive: median download speed falls to 80.07 Mbps through the morning, 27 percent below weekend levels at the same hours. Part of the problem is that UK mobile operators own few of their antenna sites, many of which sit on rooftops in built-up areas, says Ookla. Under the Electronic Communications Code, and changes introduced in 2017, a London rooftop is worth about £1,000 ($1,333) a year to its owner, down from £21,000 ($28k). That givers landlords little motivation to host antennas, and many prefer solar panels. Operators can also receive notices to quit when a building is redeveloped, and it is estimated that this keeps about 7 percent of London’s rooftop sites out of action at any time. Planning rules compound the problem as applications for new masts are more likely to be refused in boroughs with conservation areas, such as Westminster. Street mast applications peaked in 2020, early in the first 5G build, and have fallen by more than four-fifths since 2022. Three quarters of applications for new street masts since 2019 were refused, against one in five upgrades. "Planning restrictions, particularly in conservation areas, make it harder to install and upgrade the mobile equipment London needs," Ookla lead industry analyst Luke Kehoe told The Register . "Notices to quit can also force rooftop sites offline during redevelopment long before replacements are ready, leaving operators trying to restore lost capacity while demand keeps growing." City Hall has noticed, and a draft plan for the capital drawn up by the Mayor of London observes that notices to quit "have eroded London’s overall mobile connectivity compared to other equivalent cities." item.dc:creator: Dan Robinson
item.content:encoded: London's mobile network performance has slipped behind other European capitals as operators struggle to add capacity fast enough to meet demand. The city ranked seventh out of 18 in the continent for median download speed in 2021, but traffic has since expanded faster than available capacity. Other metropolises have improved; London now has the slowest speeds and the highest latency under load, according to mobile network testing firm Ookla . The research points to obstacles mobile operators face in adding extra capacity: applications for new street masts in London have fallen since 2022, and about three quarters of those filed since 2019 were refused. The Big Smoke was among the first European capitals to get 5G coverage, yet when Ookla's Q3 2026 tests found the city now has the slowest median download speed (109.43 Mbps), the slowest median upload speed (11.40 Mbps) and the highest latency under load - a measure of how the network copes with heavy use. Ookla's records show London’s 5G medina speed peaked at 200 Mbps in Q2 2021, fell as low as 102 Mbps in Q3 2023, then recovered slightly. Paris, by contrast, has stayed above 225 Mbps since mid-2021. The cause is congestion. In Central London, performance slumps on weekdays as commuters arrive: median download speed falls to 80.07 Mbps through the morning, 27 percent below weekend levels at the same hours. Part of the problem is that UK mobile operators own few of their antenna sites, many of which sit on rooftops in built-up areas, says Ookla. Under the Electronic Communications Code, and changes introduced in 2017, a London rooftop is worth about £1,000 ($1,333) a year to its owner, down from £21,000 ($28k). That givers landlords little motivation to host antennas, and many prefer solar panels. Operators can also receive notices to quit when a building is redeveloped, and it is estimated that this keeps about 7 percent of London’s rooftop sites out of action at any time. Planning rules compound the problem as applications for new masts are more likely to be refused in boroughs with conservation areas, such as Westminster. Street mast applications peaked in 2020, early in the first 5G build, and have fallen by more than four-fifths since 2022. Three quarters of applications for new street masts since 2019 were refused, against one in five upgrades. "Planning restrictions, particularly in conservation areas, make it harder to install and upgrade the mobile equipment London needs," Ookla lead industry analyst Luke Kehoe told The Register . "Notices to quit can also force rooftop sites offline during redevelopment long before replacements are ready, leaving operators trying to restore lost capacity while demand keeps growing." City Hall has noticed, and a draft plan for the capital drawn up by the Mayor of London observes that notices to quit "have eroded London’s overall mobile connectivity compared to other equivalent cities." The plan, due tor adoption in 2028, would require developers to keep mobile service running during construction, put masts on taller buildings and in the public realm; and ask boroughs to work with operators on sites in conservation areas. Other experts blame different factors for London’s poor mobile service. Professor Mohamed-Slim Alouini of the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) told The Register last year that the government’s decision to rip-and-replace network equipment supplied by China-based vendor Huawei had diverted funds that should have gone into building more capacity. He also said 5G was overhyped early on, leading to a perception among users that it wasn’t really worth having and operators reluctant to invest. Whatever the cause, London’s mobile experience now trails its European peers, though people elsewhere in the UK who still can’t get a 5G signal will have little sympathy. ®

item.title: Why cyber resilience is now a boardroom priority for UK public services
item.description: The UK public sector has reached a cyber resilience inflection point. A new Prime Minister has taken office, and significant machinery-of-government changes have already been announced, including the scrapping of DSIT, the department that had become the center of government digital, technology and cyber policy. Its responsibilities are now being redistributed across other parts of Whitehall, creating a new policy and delivery landscape for public sector leaders to navigate. For years, cyber security was treated as a specialist operational discipline that was essential but largely delegated to technical teams. That model is no longer sustainable. Pressure is now coming from three directions at once, as policy raises expectations for boards and senior leaders, organizational reform reshapes how services, systems and suppliers connect, and technology change, from cloud and hybrid work to AI, expands both opportunity and exposure. Together, these forces mean cyber resilience can no longer sit below board level. Public services, from healthcare and benefits to transport, education, local government and emergency response, are now so digitally dependent that a cyber incident is not simply an IT outage. It is a risk to public trust, public safety and the continuity of government itself. Recent history shows what this means in practice. The 2024 ransomware attack on Synnovis, a pathology services provider to parts of the NHS, significantly reduced the capacity to process blood, urine and specimen tests, caused disruption across south-east London and contributed to delays affecting more than 11,000 outpatient and elective procedure appointments. Incidents like this turn abstract cyber risk into real-world service disruption, making resilience a boardroom issue rather than a back-office concern. Cyber resilience is no longer a technical aspiration, but a leadership obligation shaped by policy, organizational and technology change. Policy change has made cyber resilience a leadership obligation The direction from government and the National Cyber Security Centre is clear. The Cyber Resilience Pledge asks organizations to make cyber security a board-level responsibility, register for NCSC Early Warning and take a risk-based approach to Cyber Essentials across their supply chains. The NCSC’s Cyber Governance Code of Practice reinforces the point that cyber risk must be governed like any other material organizational risk. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill will further expand expectations across essential and digital services, strengthening incident reporting and bringing more critical suppliers into scope. This matters because the scale and impact of cyber threats facing the UK are increasing sharply. The NCSC handled 204 nationally significant cyber incidents in the year to September 2025, up from 89 the previous year.
